name: Neo4j
license: GPLv3 (Community Edition); Enterprise Edition and AuraDB are proprietary, and Enterprise source has been closed since 3.5 (November 2018)
summary: The best-known native graph database: nodes and relationships stored as linked records, queried with Cypher, self-hosted or as AuraDB.
intro: Neo4j is a Java server that stores a property graph: nodes with labels, typed and directed relationships, and properties on both. Its own store files keep each node pointing at its list of relationships, so a query hops from node to neighbour without an index lookup, which Neo4j calls index-free adjacency. Transactions are ACID. Applications send Cypher, Neo4j’s pattern language and a major input to the ISO GQL standard, over the binary Bolt protocol (port 7687) using official drivers, or use the Browser on port 7474. Indexes find the starting nodes, including full-text indexes and HNSW vector indexes for similarity search over embeddings, often combined with traversals for GraphRAG. The Graph Data Science (GDS) library adds parallel graph algorithms such as PageRank, community detection, path finding and node embeddings, run as Cypher procedures on an in-memory projection of the graph.

Community Edition is GPLv3 and runs as a single instance with one user database. Enterprise Edition is commercial and adds clustering (each database has primaries, which keep accepting writes while a majority is up, plus read-only secondaries), online backup, multiple databases, role-based access control, change data capture and the faster block store format; sharding of a single database arrived in late 2025 for the Infinigraph edition only. AuraDB is the managed service on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, billed per GB of provisioned memory per hour: as of 6 October 2026, Professional starts at $0.09 per GB-hour (minimum 1 GB) and Business Critical at $0.20 (minimum 2 GB), with storage, IO, network and backups included. AuraDB Free costs nothing but caps node and relationship counts.
strengths: Native graph storage: multi-hop queries touch only the nodes and relationships they visit, regardless of total graph size
Cypher is mature, readable and converging on ISO GQL, with drivers for .NET, Go, Java, JavaScript and Python
Vector, full-text and graph queries in one database, all available in Community Edition
Graph Data Science library for algorithms such as PageRank and community detection, and AuraDB on all three big clouds with a free tier
limits: Community Edition has no clustering, online backup, role-based access control or multiple databases; production high availability means buying Enterprise or AuraDB
Enterprise source has been closed since 2018, and Community is GPLv3 copyleft; Neo4j won a lawsuit against a company that stripped restrictions from its earlier Enterprise licence
Writes to one database go through its primaries; splitting a single database across machines is new and limited to the Infinigraph edition
AuraDB bills provisioned memory every hour it runs; a paused instance still costs 20% of the running rate, and a Free instance pauses after 72 idle hours and is deleted after 30 days paused
Community Edition’s aligned store format caps a graph at about 34 billion nodes and relationships; the higher-limit block format is Enterprise-only

snippet.title: Run Community Edition in Docker, load a tiny graph and query two hops out
source: # once it has started (docker logs -f neo4j), run Cypher through cypher-shell
docker exec -i neo4j cypher-shell -u neo4j -p secret-password <<'EOF'
RETURN fof.name AS friend_of_friend, p.sku AS bought;
CREATE VECTOR INDEX product_embeddings IF NOT EXISTS

sections.title: Community and Enterprise
sections.intro: Both editions run the same Cypher on the same native graph engine. The differences are in availability, security, operations and scale. AuraDB runs Enterprise features as a service.

sections.title: AuraDB tiers
sections.intro: List prices from neo4j.com/pricing, checked 6 October 2026. You pay for provisioned memory per hour; at 730 hours a month, $0.09 per GB-hour is about $66 per GB of memory.

items.name: AuraDB Free
items.text: One instance per account, with caps on node and relationship counts. Pauses automatically after 72 hours without activity and is deleted if it stays paused for 30 days.

items.name: AuraDB Professional
items.text: Minimum 1 GB, up to 128 GB of memory, single zone, daily backups kept 7 days. Instances can be paused at 80% off.

items.name: AuraDB Business Critical
items.text: Minimum 2 GB, up to 512 GB on AWS and Azure or 2 TB on Google Cloud. Multi-zone with a 99.95% SLA, multiple databases, read-only secondaries, change data capture, 30-day backups with point-in-time restore.

items.name: AuraDB Virtual Dedicated Cloud
items.text: Business Critical features on dedicated, VPC-isolated infrastructure, with hourly backups kept 60 days.

story: Around 2000, Emil Eifrem, Johan Svensson and Peter Neubauer were building a content management system in Sweden and kept running into the performance limits of relational databases for connected data. They built a graph engine instead, ran it in production around the clock from 2003, and in 2007 formed Neo Technology and released Neo4j under the GPL. Version 1.0 followed in 2010, and the company moved its headquarters to Silicon Valley in 2011.

Cypher, Neo4j’s pattern language, dates from 2010. In 2015 Neo4j opened it as openCypher, backed by Oracle, Databricks and others, and Neo4j engineers later spent about five years on the ISO committee that published GQL in 2024.

Licensing caused the most friction. Enterprise Edition had been released under the AGPL; for 3.4 Neo4j added the Commons Clause, and from 3.5 in November 2018 it stopped publishing Enterprise source altogether. PureThink and its founder John Mark Suhy removed the Commons Clause and kept offering the code. A federal court found the defendants liable under trademark law and the DMCA and in July 2024 awarded Neo4j $597,000 plus a permanent injunction; the defendants appealed to the Ninth Circuit.

choices.choice: Native graph storage instead of a layer over tables
choices.why: The founders started Neo4j because relational databases were too slow for their connected data, so relationships are stored records that a query follows directly.

choices.choice: A query language modelled on SQL
choices.why: Cypher followed a “no idle variance from SQL” principle, adding ASCII-art patterns only where graphs needed them. That made it a natural input to GQL.

choices.choice: Open core: GPL Community, commercial Enterprise
choices.why: Neo4j said in 2018 that it wanted to stop confusion about which parts of its code it sells and which it gives away, so Enterprise became commercial-only while Community stayed GPLv3.

timeline.text: The founders build a first graph prototype after hitting relational limits
Neo Technology is formed in Sweden; Neo4j is released under the GPL
Enterprise Edition goes closed source from 3.5; Neo4j sues PureThink
AuraDB, the managed cloud service, launches
ISO publishes GQL; the court awards Neo4j $597,000 against PureThink
